thread.title: Russia Admits Only 68% of Trade with Iran Settled in Local Currency, Contradicting 95% Claim

author: HeadTopics.com
title: Russia Admits Only 68% of Trade with Iran Settled in Local Currency, Contradicting 95% Claim
text:
A leaked Russian government document reveals that just 68% of trade with Iran is settled in rubles and rials, contradicting public claims by President Putin and Iranian officials that nearly all bilateral trade has been shifted away from the dollar. The discrepancy highlights the challenges of maintaining a stable non-dollar trade system due to currency imbalances and lack of convertibility, while U.S. sanctions continue to target financial institutions facilitating these transactions.
A leaked Russian government roadmap obtained by Fox News reveals that only 68% of trade with Iran is settled using the currencies of the two countries - far below Moscow's public claim that nearly all bilateral trade has been shifted to rubles and rials.
تحریمهای جدید آمریکا علیه شبکه مالی ایران
The effort to remove the dollar from trade settlements has once again attracted U.S. attention. The U.S. Treasury Department imposed new sanctions on Russia's VTB Bank last month, citing the bank's role in establishing the ruble-rial settlement system as part of the reason for the move. On Thursday, the Treasury Department targeted the Russia-affiliated A7 network, describing it as a 'shadow banking network' used by the Iranian regime to evade sanctions.
The Treasury said A7 affiliates created a money-laundering and sanctions-evasion mechanism linked to Russian illicit financial activities, which the Iranian regime used to transfer funds, including oil revenues and money needed to buy weapons. The Iranian and Russian governments have for years insisted they do not need the dollar.
However, declaring a percentage of trade settled in local currencies only makes sense when the goal is to convince others that sanctions have no effect. The leverage of sanctions works only if others believe it exists.
To create the impression that such leverage does not exist, Russia has reported an increasing share of its trade with Iran being settled in rubles and rials since 2019 - starting at 40%, then 50%, 60%, and 80%, until President Putin declared it at 95% in January 2025. Iran, instead of issuing quarterly statistical reports like the Soviet Union, makes its claims in vague statements.
تضاد ادعای بانک مرکزی با اسناد داخلی
The governor of Iran's central bank said in November 2024 that Iran has 'completely removed the dollar' and that trade is conducted only in rubles and rials. But an internal document adopted in September 2024 shows the real figure is 68%, with a target of 71% for 2026.
Defending the Kremlin's claim that the ruble-rial payment system is working becomes more difficult when there is an imbalance in trade between the two countries, as this imbalance can cause one side to lack sufficient currency to cover demand. Russian statistics for 2023 show bilateral trade at about $4 billion, including $2.7 billion in Russian exports and $1.3 billion in Iranian exports. Neither country is particularly eager to hold the other's currency.
The Russian Central Bank described currencies like the rial in 2023 as 'often non-convertible or partially convertible,' suffering from 'higher volatility,' and traded in markets lacking sufficient depth for risk hedging. According to an Iranian economic institute, Iranian exporters avoid accepting rubles whenever possible, and if they do, they convert them to dirhams as quickly as possible.
The standard solution to such shortages is a currency swap line between central banks - an agreement signed by Iran and Russia in July 2024. However, two years later, the only publicly mentioned contribution is a 1 billion ruble deposit in VTB Bank, which at the time of deposit was worth about $10 million and intended to cover 'expected ruble shortages.
' Any further drawdowns from this line would leave Russia holding rials as collateral - a currency that cannot be sold in Russia and has lost 29% of its value against the ruble since January. A member of Iran's parliament says Russia has offered a $20 billion loan in rubles, but Iran has not taken it. If the ruble-rial system worked as advertised, Iranian merchants would not need to pay Dubai and Turkish exchange houses for access to Russian suppliers.
توسعه بازارهای موازی ارزی در خلیج فارس
MP Meisam Zahourian told the Fars news agency in June that even before the war, essential goods bought from Russia were shipped through the UAE and paid for in dirhams. Fars asked in August why merchants continue to settle trade with Russia through exchange houses and trusted individuals in Turkey.
The governor of Iran's central bank described his June trip to Moscow as an 'operational mission to untie the knots' in foreign trade, saying the first step is to open letters of credit for Iranian merchants. Whatever figures are reported do not necessarily measure the actual money moving between Iran and Russia. They are accounting tools that record which currency leaves a Russian company's account, not what currency the other side eventually receives.
If a Russian importer's bank debits rubles, converts them to dollars, and pays the seller in dollars, the Russian central bank will count that as a ruble settlement - even if the contract is priced in dollars and the seller received dollars. These statistics also ignore trades arranged without traditional cross-border payments.
